extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts definitions, equivalences, examples, and exercises about Picard groups, class groups, effective Cartier divisors, globally generated sheaves, very ample/ample line bundles, and related algebraic criteria. Useful as a checklist of facts/criteria one should know or verify when working with these notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excision exact sequence for class groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking into account the fact that we may lose exactness on the left, we get an excision exact sequence for class groups: Z[Z] → Cl X → Cl(X − Z) → 0 (see (15.4.11.1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly to relate class groups of a scheme and the complement of a closed subscheme; see exercises that apply it to compute Pic/Cl in examples (e.g., hypersurfaces, cones). Note warning about possible loss of exactness on the left.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard group of an open subscheme of affine space
rubrics_metrics.description: For example, if U is an open subscheme of X = A^n, Pic U = {0}. (15.4.12)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic fact used as a reality-check and tool: invertible sheaves on affine space (and opens thereof) are trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard and class groups of projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: For X = P^n_k and Z the hyperplane x_0 = 0, one gets Pic(P^n_k) ≅ Z with generator O(1); define deg O(d) = d. The class [Z] generates Cl P^n_k and is not torsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the standard computation Pic(P^n)=Z and the degree map. Exercises demonstrate non-torsion and how restriction to subschemes can detect nontriviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: factorial Noetherian scheme gives Pic ≅ Cl
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is Noetherian and factorial, then for any Weil divisor D, O(D) is invertible, and hence the map Pic X → Cl X is an isomorphism. (15.4.15)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to connect class groups to Picard groups in factorial (e.g., regular) situations; used to relate arithmetic class groups to geometric class groups (see exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Twisting line bundles by divisors (definition of L(D))
rubrics_metrics.description: Let L be an invertible sheaf on a normal Noetherian scheme X. Define L(D) := O_X(D) ⊗ L. Sections of L(D) can be interpreted both as sections of the new line bundle and as rational sections of L with poles/zeros constrained by D. (15.4.16)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two viewpoints (geometric sheaf vs rational sections with divisor bounds) are both useful; exercise 15.4.L makes the translation explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of sections of L(D) as rational sections with divisor constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: (Exercise 15.4.L(a)) Assuming X irreducible: Γ(U, L(D)) := {t nonzero rational section of L : div|_U t + D|_U ≥ {0}}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete criterion to check whether a rational section belongs to Γ(U,L(D)); used when computing global sections and understanding twists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility of twisting: O(D1)(D2) ≅ O(D1 + D2)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Exercise 15.4.L(b)) If D1 and D2 are locally principal, then (O(D1))(D2) ≅ O(D1 + D2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows twisting by divisors behaves like addition of divisors; useful algebraic identity when manipulating line bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of invertible sheaves and effective Cartier divisors to subschemes
rubrics_metrics.description: You can restrict invertible sheaves on Y to any subscheme X; effective Cartier divisors sometimes restrict to effective Cartier divisors on X provided the local defining equation does not vanish at associated points of X. Restriction corresponds to restriction of invertible sheaves. (15.4.17)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique to prove nontriviality of restricted bundles; check associated points to ensure Cartier property persists under restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard group of complement of a hypersurface (torsion example)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y ⊂ P^n_k is an irreducible hypersurface of degree d, then Pic(P^n_k − Y) ≅ Z/(d). (Exercise 15.4.M)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives many concrete torsion Picard groups; for topologists relates to π1 phenomena. Used to produce examples where Pic is nontrivial but has torsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affineness and failure of UFD being affine-local
rubrics_metrics.description: For Y a hypersurface of degree d>1, P^n − Y is affine, and distinguished open subsets P^n − Y − H_i are Specs of UFDs, but P^n − Y is not a UFD. Thus unique factorization property is not affine-local (fails one hypothesis of the Affine Communication Lemma). (Exercise 15.4.N/O)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important caution: UFD property does not glue from affine opens; use Pic/Cl computations to detect global failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base-change can change UFD property (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: A := R[x,y]/(x^2 + y^2 − 1) is not a UFD, but A ⊗_R C is. (Exercise 15.4.P)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that passing to algebraic closure or other base change can change factorization properties; check via prior exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard group of a smooth quadric surface (product P^1 × P^1 example)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ≅ P^1_k ×_k P^1_k (a smooth quadric surface), then Pic X ≅ Z ⊕ Z with generators given by the two rulings; explicit descriptions via divisors L and M and their restrictions. (Exercise 15.4.Q)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computations of Pic for products and quadrics often yield rank-2 Picard groups and are instructive examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard detects birational but non-isomorphic surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Irreducible smooth projective surfaces over k can be birational but not isomorphic; Picard groups (e.g., P^2 vs P^1 × P^1) can distinguish them. (Exercise 15.4.R)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picard group is an invariant powerful enough to detect non-isomorphism among birational surfaces; motivates blow-up analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: cone with Pic = 0 but Cl ≅ Z/2
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X = Spec k[x,y,z]/(xy − z^2) (cone). Then Pic X = 0 and Cl X ≅ Z/2; the class of Z = {x = z = 0} generates Cl X and 2[Z] is principal. (Exercise 15.4.S)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibits that Pic and Cl can differ and that removing codimension ≥2 loci may change Pic but not Cl.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Q-Cartier and example of non-Q-Cartier divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: A Weil divisor with a nonzero multiple corresponding to a line bundle is called Q-Cartier. There exist Weil divisors that are not Q-Cartier (exercise 15.4.T gives an explicit example on a cone over a quadric surface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check non-Q-Cartierness show that no multiple is locally principal, often by looking at complements and affineness of closed subschemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of ideal class group of ring of integers with geometric class group
rubrics_metrics.description: (Exercise 15.4.U) The ideal class group of the ring of integers O_K in a number field K identifies with the class group of Spec O_K; recovers the classical description as formal sums of prime ideals modulo principal fractional ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important bridge between algebraic number theory and geometric class groups; use the scheme-theoretic definition of Cl and compare with ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of UFD via integrally closed + trivial class group
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A is a Noetherian integral domain. Then A is a UFD if and only if A is integrally closed and Cl Spec A = 0. (Exercise 15.4.V)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One direction is straightforward; the other uses that codimension-1 primes are principal iff Cl=0 and integrally closedness to lift factorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nagata's Lemma (criterion for UFD)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Exercise 15.4.W) If A is Noetherian domain and x∈A is such that (x) is prime and A[1/x] is a UFD, then A is a UFD. Use the short exact sequence Z[(x)] → Cl Spec A → Cl Spec A_x → 0 to conclude Cl Spec A = 0 and check integral closedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful induction trick: invert a prime element whose complement is UFD to deduce global UFD; see hint on integral dependence and contrapositive arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qcqs Lemma variation: extending sections after multiplying by powers of a section
rubrics_metrics.description: (Exercise 15.4.Y) Suppose X is quasicompact quasiseparated, L invertible with section s, and F quasicoherent. Let X_s be where s doesn't vanish. Any section of F over X_s can be written as quotient of a global section of F ⊗ L^n by s^n (i.e., multiplied by high enough power of s extends it globally); moreover one gets an isomorphism between the graded constructions described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard technique of clearing denominators using a global section, formulated in graded language; key tool for local-to-global arguments on projective-type schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of effective Cartier divisors (ideal sheaf invertible)
rubrics_metrics.description: D ⊂ X is an effective Cartier divisor iff its ideal sheaf I is invertible; equivalently locally I≅A generated by a single element a which is a non-zerodivisor, i.e., locally cut out by one non-zerodivisor. In the locally Noetherian case: locally cut out by one equation not vanishing at any associated point. (15.5 and 9.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an intrinsic scheme-theoretic criterion to recognize Cartier divisors; check non-zerodivisor condition or associated points in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of O(D) for effective Cartier divisor and canonical section s_D
rubrics_metrics.description: For an effective Cartier divisor D with ideal sheaf I_D, one has O(−D) = I_D and O(D) = I_D^∨ (dual). There is a canonical section s_D cutting out D, and the closed-subscheme exact sequence 0 → O(−D) → O → O_D → 0 holds. (15.5.B–D)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use duality to define O(D); exercise shows s_D indeed cuts out D. The correspondence is reversible: a line bundle with a section non-zerodivisor cuts out an effective Cartier divisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of invertible ideal sheaves correspond to sums of Cartier divisors
rubrics_metrics.description: If I and J are invertible ideal sheaves corresponding to effective Cartier divisors D and D′, then IJ is invertible and corresponds to D + D′; O(D + D′) ≅ O(D) ⊗ O(D′). (15.5.E)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a semigroup homomorphism from effective Cartier divisors to invertible sheaves with sections; typical algebraic identities used in divisor arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal (line) bundle to an effective Cartier divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: If D is an effective Cartier divisor on X, the restriction O_X(D)|_D is called the normal (line) bundle N_{D/X} := O_X(D)|_D. For smooth complex varieties this matches the differential-geometric normal bundle. (15.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for deformation-theoretic and intersection-theoretic computations; intuition from geometry carries over in nonsingular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most invertible sheaves arise as differences of effective Cartier divisors (typical but not universal)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many reasonable circumstances (regular or factorial schemes, projective schemes, finite-type k-schemes) every invertible sheaf can be written as difference of two effective Cartier divisors; there are exceptions (Kleiman's example). (15.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: to construct invertible sheaves, look for effective divisors; but be aware of pathological counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of globally generated (generated by global sections) sheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasicoherent sheaf F on X is globally generated if there is a surjection O_X^{⊕I} → F (i.e., images of global sections generate all stalks). If I can be finite, F is finitely globally generated. Local version: generated at a point p if surjection on stalks at p holds. (16.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent fiber criterion: for finite type F, F is globally generated at p iff global sections span the fiber F ⊗ k(p) (Geometric Nakayama). Global generation is local in p and, on quasicompact spaces, finite global generation ⇔ global generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic closure properties of globally generated sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct sums and tensor products of globally generated sheaves are globally generated; if F and G are globally generated then F ⊗ G is as well. (Exercises 16.1.A–B)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to build new globally generated bundles from known ones (noting finite generation if constituents are finite type).

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's Theorem A (global generation of twists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose S is a finitely generated graded algebra generated in degree 1 over A. For any finite type quasicoherent sheaf F on Proj S, there exists n_0 such that for all n ≥ n_0, F(n) is finitely globally generated. (16.1.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental result used to present coherent sheaves as quotients of sums of O(−n); key tool in projective geometry and cohomology vanishing approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of finite type sheaves on Proj as quotient of sums of twists of O
rubrics_metrics.description: (Theorem 16.1.1) Any finite type quasicoherent sheaf F on Proj S can be presented as ⊕_{finite} O(-n_i) → F → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate corollary of Serre's Theorem A; allows hands-on manipulations with coherent sheaves on projective schemes and leads to syzygy/resolution statements (Hilbert Syzygy Theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of very ample line bundle (relative/over A)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invertible sheaf L on X (over Spec A) is very ample over A (π-very ample) if X ≅ Proj S for some finitely generated graded A-algebra S generated in degree 1 and L ≅ O_{Proj S}(1). Equivalently (for proper X), there exist finitely many global sections s_0,...,s_n with no common zeros such that [s_0:...:s_n]: X → P^n_A is a closed embedding. (16.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being very ample gives an explicit embedding into projective space; useful equivalent characterization via global sections and closed embedding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very ample implies base-point-free; base-point-free criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is very ample on a proper A-scheme X, then L is base-point-free: for every p ∈ X there is a section of L not vanishing at p. (Exercise 16.2.B and related)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base-point-freeness is a necessary (but not sufficient) condition for very ampleness; checking local nonvanishing of a section tests base-point-freeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor and product rules for very ample sheaves (Segre/Cancellation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is very ample and M is base-point-free on a proper A-scheme, then L ⊗ M is very ample (via Segre embedding arguments and Cancellation Theorem). Also pullbacks and external tensor products of very ample bundles on proper schemes behave well (Exercises 16.2.C–D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques to produce new very ample bundles from existing ones, using product embeddings and Segre embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ample line bundle and equivalent criteria (Theorem 16.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: L invertible on proper A-scheme X is ample (relative to π : X → Spec A) iff any of the following equivalent conditions hold: (a) some N>0 with L^{⊗N} very ample over A (equivalently for all n ≫ 0, L^{⊗n} very ample); (b) for every finite-type quasicoherent sheaf F, ∃ n_0 s.t. for n ≥ n_0, F ⊗ L^{⊗n} is globally generated; (c) the open subsets X_f (as f runs through global sections of L^{⊗n}, all n>0) form a base for the topology of X; variants: those X_f that are affine form a base or cover X. (16.2.1–16.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central list of equivalent characterizations of ampleness: projective-geometry criterion, asymptotic global generation, and topology/affineness criteria. Use whichever is most convenient for proofs/applications (e.g., (b) for cohomological methods, (c) for topological/affine-local arguments). Also ampleness is an open condition in families and relates to cohomological criteria (Serre/Kodaira).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ample twist makes bundles very ample for high powers
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is ample on a proper A-scheme X and M any invertible sheaf, then for n ≫ 0 the twist L^{⊗n} ⊗ M is very ample. (Important Exercise 16.2.E, standard consequence of Theorem 16.2.2.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard practical tool: by taking sufficiently high powers of an ample bundle and twisting by any fixed line bundle, one achieves very ampleness — used to produce embeddings and projective models.
